My daughter, Claire, had been slipping out at odd hours, returning home with scrapes and bruises she couldn’t explain. I had dismissed them as playground mishaps or schoolyard scuffles. But as I snapped open the locket, my stomach clenched. A soft, ethereal glow pulsed from its center, and then—

A voice, celestial and calm, filled the room. 

“Moon Guardian, your presence is acknowledged.”

I nearly dropped the thing. “Moon Guardian? No, no, you’ve got the wrong person. I’m her mother.”

There was a pause, then the voice returned, slightly bemused. “Parental figure of the Moon Guardian, how may I assist you?”

“Oh, I’ll tell you how,” I snapped, my grip tightening around the locket. “You sent my *fourteen-year-old daughter* to fight cosmic horrors! What part of that sounds remotely acceptable to you?”

Another pause. Then, a different voice—softer, yet commanding—echoed from the locket. “I am the Moon Goddess. Your concerns are heard.”

“Oh, they’d better be,” I huffed. “She is *fourteen*. She still forgets to put the milk back in the fridge. And you’ve got her fighting intergalactic monstrosities?”

“She has been chosen,” the Moon Goddess intoned. “Her courage, her heart, her destiny—”

“She’s a *kid*,” I interrupted. “She has a math test on Monday. Destiny doesn’t cover algebra.”

A sigh, reverberating like wind through ancient trees. “She is stronger than you know.”

I pinched the bridge of my nose. “That’s not the point! Look, I get it. The world needs heroes. But why children? Why not someone who’s already been through puberty at least?”

The locket dimmed, as if the deity inside was contemplating my words. “The young have the purest hearts,” she finally said. “They believe in justice without cynicism, in hope without hesitation.”

I exhaled sharply. “Yeah, well, they also believe in staying up past bedtime and eating cereal for dinner.”

“Would you deny her destiny?”

I hesitated. Claire had always been special—brave, selfless, more than I ever gave her credit for. But she was still my little girl. My job was to keep her safe, not send her into battle. 

“What if she gets hurt?” I asked, voice barely above a whisper.

The Moon Goddess’s voice softened. “She will rise. She will fall. But she will never stand alone.”

Tears burned at the corners of my eyes. “She has me, too.”

“And that,” the Moon Goddess murmured, “is why she is unstoppable.”

The locket’s glow faded. My heart ached, but I knew one thing for certain—I’d be having a long talk with Claire. And the next time she ran off to fight the forces of darkness, she wouldn’t be going alone.

I hesitated for a moment, feeling a strange guilt coil in my stomach. What if it was worse than I remembered? What if it didn’t match the pages they’d shared with me, and I found myself cringing through every line?

*Stop it,* I told myself. This was about them, not me. 

With a breath, I reached out and pulled the book from the shelf. The cover felt cool and smooth under my fingers, and I marveled at how far my partner had come. They’d always dreamed of this, even when their words had seemed like foreign language to me. I couldn’t help but be proud, no matter my own indifference to the content. You brush off your wife's new strange behaviour after the murder as grief. Until you find an old family photo of your wife as a kid, you shiver as you realise... they're twins.
text:
The house felt different these days. The air, once familiar and comforting, now carried a weight—something I couldn’t quite name. Perhaps it was the grief. Maybe it was the silence that lingered between my wife, Emma, and me, growing ever so thick after the news came in about her sister, Charlotte. 

I had never met Charlotte. I knew of her, of course—how could I not? Emma spoke of her in the past, with a bittersweet nostalgia that hinted at stories untold. But after the wedding, it was as if Charlotte had vanished from the family narrative, a shadow no one spoke of, not even Emma. The silence was her decision. I respected it, let her bury her memories wherever they would fit in her heart, never prying, never pushing.

That was, until the day they found her.

The news was swift, clinical, and unfathomable. Charlotte had been found, her case reopened after years of no progress. Murdered. The details were scarce, a cold case reopened with no answers to offer. Emma, shaken but composed, became a shell of herself. I thought I understood grief—I thought I could carry her through it. 

But she slipped further away each day, retreating into herself in ways that left me feeling like an intruder in our own home. She stayed up late, eyes hollow and unfocused, as if she was staring into a world I couldn’t see. Sometimes, I’d wake to find her standing by the window in the dead of night, her face illuminated only by the dim glow of streetlights. She wouldn’t speak when I asked her what was wrong, only offering me a tight smile that didn’t quite reach her eyes.

I brushed it off, told myself it was just grief. 

Until one day, when I found something I never expected. 

I was in the attic, cleaning out some boxes of old family keepsakes Emma had been meaning to sort through. There were photo albums, yellowed pages filled with memories, snapshots of lives before my time. I flipped through the pages, not thinking much of it, until one photograph caught my eye. It was a black-and-white image of two young girls, arms draped around each other, smiling into the camera. Their faces were sweet, innocent, as children’s faces should be. One had Emma’s dark eyes and the same brown hair I knew so well. But the other—the other had the same face, the same eyes, the same laugh lines. 

The same smile.

I froze, heart thudding in my chest, a chill crawling up my spine. My fingers trembled as I turned the photo over. On the back was a simple note in Emma’s handwriting: “Charlotte and me, 6 years old.”

I blinked, as if the world might shift if I closed my eyes long enough. But when I opened them again, the photo was still there, glaring at me with its unmistakable truth. They weren’t just sisters. They were twins.

A memory flickered—Emma’s insistence, years ago, that Charlotte had been *gone* long before the murder, that her absence was just a part of the family’s quiet grief. But no one had ever said they were twins. Not once. 

My stomach twisted, and a deep unease settled in my bones. How had I not known? How had I missed this? And why—why hadn’t Emma told me? 

I heard footsteps behind me, soft but deliberate. I turned to see her standing in the doorway, her face pale, lips pressed tight.

“I thought you might find that,” she said, her voice barely a whisper. “I thought you might remember.”

I couldn’t breathe. The silence between us stretched out, thick with unspoken words. Emma’s eyes locked onto mine, and for the first time, I saw something there that I hadn’t before—something darker than grief. Something buried too deep for even me to reach.

“Emma,” I said, but my voice faltered, uncertain of what to say next.

She stepped forward, a small, sad smile tugging at her lips. "I didn’t want you to know," she said softly. "Not yet."

premise: The world ended 20 years ago, you haven't found a living soul since then. Through some ingenuity, you call voicemails for the last 20 years to keep you company. ""Hi, this is Cindy..."" ""Hi you reached Bob"" ""You know what to do at the beep"" until one day ""Hello...hello? Oh my God hello!""
text:
The world ended quietly, not with a bang, but with a slow unraveling. One day, the streets were full of life; the next, they were empty. I don’t know what happened to everyone. I only know that I woke up one morning, and the silence was deafening. That was twenty years ago. Since then, I’ve been alone.

At first, I searched. I called out, hoping to hear a voice, any voice, in return. But there was nothing. Just the echo of my own words bouncing off crumbling buildings and overgrown streets. Eventually, I stopped searching. I stopped calling out. But I couldn’t stop longing for connection.

That’s when I found the old phone booth. It was a relic, a rusted metal box with a cracked glass pane, but it still worked. I don’t know how, but it did. And so, I began calling numbers—any numbers I could remember. Most were disconnected, of course. But some still had voicemails. Little fragments of lives long gone. 

“Hi, this is Cindy. Leave a message, and I’ll call you back!” Her voice was bright, cheerful. I imagined her smiling as she recorded it, her hair bouncing as she spoke. I called her number every day, just to hear her voice.

“Hi, you’ve reached Bob. I’m probably out fishing or tinkering in the garage. Leave a message, and I’ll get back to you.” Bob sounded like the kind of man who wore flannel shirts and fixed things with his hands. I wondered if he ever caught the big one.

“You know what to do at the beep.” That one was curt, no-nonsense. I called it when I needed a reminder that not everyone was warm and welcoming. It grounded me.

These voicemails became my companions. I memorized every inflection, every pause. They were my tether to humanity, to a world that once was. I’d sit in that phone booth for hours, dialing numbers, listening to the voices of the dead. It was the closest thing to company I had.

But then, one day, something changed.

I dialed a number at random, as I always did. The line clicked, and I braced myself for the familiar robotic voice telling me the number was no longer in service. But instead, I heard something else.

“Hello… hello?” A voice, faint and trembling, came through the receiver. My heart stopped. “Oh my God, hello!”

I couldn’t speak. My throat tightened, and my hands shook so badly I almost dropped the phone. It had been twenty years since I’d heard a voice that wasn’t a recording. Twenty years of silence. And now, this.

“Hello?” the voice said again, more desperate this time. “Is anyone there?”

“Yes,” I finally managed to croak. “Yes, I’m here.”

There was a pause, and then a sob. “I thought I was the only one,” the voice said. “I thought I was alone.”

“So did I,” I whispered. 

We talked for hours, our words spilling out in a torrent of relief and disbelief. Her name was Elena. She had been living in an underground bunker, surviving on canned goods and rainwater. She had found an old radio and had been broadcasting messages for years, hoping someone would hear her. She had almost given up hope.

When we finally hung up, I sat in the phone booth for a long time, staring at the receiver. The world was still empty, still broken. But for the first time in twenty years, I didn’t feel alone. 

And that was enough.

text:
The morning sun filtered through the canopy of oaks, casting dappled light on the rows of hives that stood like sentinels in the meadow. As I lifted the lid of the first hive, the usual chorus of buzzing shifted in tone. It wasn’t the usual industrious hum but something more deliberate, almost… conversational. I paused, listening. The bees swirled around me, their movements precise, almost choreographed. And then, faintly, I felt it—a sensation, not quite words, but a clear impression forming in my mind.

*We need to talk.*

I blinked, startled. The bees had always communicated with me in subtle ways—a shift in their vibrations, a pattern in their flight—but this was different. This was direct. I crouched beside the hive, my heart pounding. “What is it?” I whispered, though I knew they didn’t need words to understand me.

The response came in a flood of images and emotions. I saw their hives, not as I knew them, but as they saw them: cramped, aging, struggling to support their growing numbers. I felt their frustration, their determination. And then, clear as day, the message crystallized in my mind.

*The new queens have decided. We need better hives. Stronger. Bigger. You must invest.*

I sat back on my heels, stunned. Invest? The idea was absurd, and yet… I looked around at the rows of hives, some of which had stood here for decades. They were weathered, their wood warped and cracked. I had always patched them up, made do, but the bees were right. They deserved better.

“I don’t have much money,” I said aloud, my voice trembling. “I can’t just—”

The bees swarmed closer, their hum intensifying. Images flashed in my mind again: honey flowing like gold, the hives thriving, the queens strong and fertile. They weren’t asking for charity; they were proposing a partnership. If I invested in their future, they would ensure mine.

I swallowed hard, my mind racing. Beekeeping had always been a labor of love, not profit. But this… this was different. This was a leap of faith, a promise to grow together. I looked down at the hive, at the bees circling my hands like tiny, golden guardians.

“Alright,” I said softly. “I’ll do it.”

The hum shifted again, warmer now, almost grateful. I felt a surge of determination, not just from them, but from within myself. This wasn’t just about honey or hives; it was about trust, about honoring the bond we shared.

As I closed the hive and moved to the next, I felt a strange sense of anticipation. The bees had always been my teachers, showing me the delicate balance of nature, the importance of patience and care. Now, they were showing me something new: the courage to change, to grow.

And as I walked back to the house, the sun warm on my face, I knew this year would be unlike any other. Together, we would build something extraordinary.

"Finally," people said, "a way to hold them accountable." But accountability, it turned out, was a double-edged sword. Politicians, once larger-than-life figures, now scurried like rats in the shadows, desperate to avoid the collective disdain of the public. The more visible they were, the more they were downvoted. Mara stood at the window of her small apartment, staring out at the rain-soaked city. Her fingers trembled as she clutched her voting device, a sleek black rectangle no bigger than a credit card. She had spent weeks agonizing over her decision. The candidates were faceless, nameless entities, their policies reduced to sterile bullet points on a screen. No speeches, no debates, no interviews. Just words on a page, stripped of all personality. It was democracy in its purest form—or so they said.

But Mara couldn't shake the feeling that something was missing. The human element, perhaps. The messy, flawed, emotional core of what it meant to lead. She thought of her father, a man who had once believed in the power of change, who had campaigned tirelessly for a better world. He had lost, of course. The Downvote had seen to that. His face, his passion, his conviction—all of it had been too much. Too real. The public had turned on him like a pack of wolves, reducing his votes to a negative number that still haunted Mara's dreams.

She glanced at the device in her hand. The screen displayed two options: UPVOTE and DOWNVOTE. No names, no faces, just a list of policies. She had read them all, over and over, searching for some hint of humanity. But there was nothing. Just words. Cold, impersonal, and utterly devoid of soul.

Her finger hovered over the DOWNVOTE button. It would be so easy. One tap, and she could subtract her voice from the cacophony of disdain. But what would it accomplish? Another faceless figure reduced to nothing, another empty seat in a government that no one believed in anymore. She thought of her father again, of the light in his eyes when he spoke of hope, of change. That light had been extinguished by the Downvote, but it had once burned so brightly.

Mara took a deep breath and pressed UPVOTE. It was a small act of defiance, a tiny spark in the darkness. She didn't know who she was voting for, or what they stood for. But she refused to let the world become a place where hope was punished, where passion was a liability. The rain continued to fall, washing away the grime of the city, but Mara stood tall, her decision made. In a world of shadows, she had chosen to believe in the light.

text:
The dog arrived on a Tuesday, wrapped in a silence so heavy it seemed to bend the air around him. His name was Max, according to the paperwork, but he didn’t respond to it. He didn’t respond to much of anything. He was a golden retriever, or at least he looked like one, though his fur was matted and his eyes were dull, as if someone had turned down the brightness on his soul. The agency had promised me a service dog to help with my depression, but when Max shuffled into my apartment, tail limp and head hanging low, I realized something was terribly wrong.

The first few days were a quiet kind of chaos. I had expected Max to nudge me out of bed, to bark at me until I took him for walks, to remind me that life was worth living. Instead, he lay on the floor, his body curled into a tight ball, his breathing shallow and resigned. I sat beside him, my own chest heavy with the weight of a thousand unshed tears, and wondered if we were both broken beyond repair.

But then, on the fourth day, something shifted. I woke up to the sound of Max whining softly, a sound so fragile it seemed to come from the very edges of his being. I dragged myself out of bed and found him staring at the wall, his body trembling. I knelt beside him, my own despair momentarily forgotten, and placed a hand on his back. His fur was warm, but his body felt like it was carrying the weight of the world.

“Hey,” I whispered, my voice cracking. “It’s okay. I’m here.”

He didn’t look at me, but he leaned into my touch, just slightly. It was the smallest of gestures, but it was enough. For the first time in months, I felt something other than numbness. I felt needed.

From that day on, Max became my reason to get up in the morning. I fed him, even when I couldn’t bring myself to eat. I took him for walks, even though the world outside felt like a minefield of triggers. I brushed his fur, untangling the knots one by one, as if I could somehow brush away the sadness that clung to him. And slowly, as I cared for him, I began to care for myself.

There were days when it felt impossible. Days when Max would refuse to move, and I would sit beside him, crying because I didn’t know how to fix him. But even on those days, there was a strange kind of comfort in knowing that I wasn’t alone. Max understood my pain in a way no one else could. He didn’t try to cheer me up or tell me to “look on the bright side.” He just stayed with me, his quiet presence a reminder that it was okay to not be okay.

Over time, we began to heal together. Max started to wag his tail, just a little, when I came home. He began to eat without me coaxing him. And one day, as we sat in the park, he looked at me—really looked at me—and I saw a flicker of light in his eyes. It was small, but it was there.

I don’t know if Max will ever be the happy, carefree dog I imagined when I first applied for a service animal. And I don’t know if I’ll ever be free of the shadows that linger in my mind. But what I do know is this: sometimes, the thing that saves you isn’t what you expect. Sometimes, it’s not about being fixed. It’s about finding someone who understands your brokenness and choosing to carry the weight together.

Max isn’t just my service dog. He’s my companion, my mirror, my reminder that even in the darkest places, there is love. And maybe, just maybe, that’s enough.

When you ask what good deed got you into heaven you are informed that this is hell, followed by a visit from a very concerned demon.
text:
The first thing I noticed was the light. It wasn’t the harsh, blinding glare I’d always imagined heaven would have. It was soft, golden, like the glow of a late afternoon sun filtering through autumn leaves. The air smelled faintly of lavender and fresh rain, and the ground beneath my feet felt like cool grass, though I couldn’t see it clearly. Everything was hazy, like a dream I didn’t want to wake up from.

People wandered around, smiling. Not the forced, polite smiles of the living, but genuine, effortless ones. They nodded at me as they passed, their eyes warm and inviting. No one rushed. No one shouted. There was no tension in the air, no undercurrent of anxiety. It was… peaceful. More peaceful than anything I’d ever known.

I approached a woman sitting on a bench, her face serene as she watched the horizon. “Excuse me,” I said, my voice trembling slightly. “Is this… heaven?”

She turned to me, her smile widening. “It’s whatever you need it to be,” she replied. Her voice was melodic, soothing. “But yes, most people call it that.”

I frowned. “But… I don’t understand. I wasn’t… I wasn’t a good person. I mean, I wasn’t terrible, but I wasn’t saintly either. What did I do to deserve this?”

Her expression didn’t change, but there was a flicker of something in her eyes—pity, maybe. “You’ll find out soon enough,” she said gently. “But for now, just enjoy it.”

I wandered further, my mind racing. The more I saw, the more I realized how perfect it all was. There were no deadlines, no bills, no expectations. No one judged me. No one demanded anything of me. It was everything I’d ever wanted in life but never had.

Then, a man approached me. He was tall, with sharp features and eyes that glowed faintly red. He looked out of place here, his presence unsettling in this sea of tranquility. “You’re new,” he said, his voice low and gravelly.

I nodded, suddenly nervous. “Yes. I just… arrived.”

He studied me for a moment, then sighed. “I’m sorry,” he said, and he sounded genuinely regretful. “This must be confusing for you.”

“What do you mean?” I asked, my heart starting to race.

“This isn’t heaven,” he said bluntly. “This is hell.”

I laughed, a short, nervous burst of sound. “No, it’s not. This can’t be hell. Hell is supposed to be… fire and brimstone. Pain and suffering. This is… perfect.”

“Exactly,” he said, his gaze piercing. “This is your hell. Eternal peace. Eternal comfort. No challenges, no growth, no purpose. Just… endless contentment.”

I stared at him, my mind reeling. “But… why? Why would this be hell?”

“Because,” he said, his voice softening, “you were always running. Always striving. You never let yourself rest, never let yourself be still. You were so afraid of failure, of not being enough, that you never allowed yourself to just… be. And now, you’ll have eternity to do nothing but that. No goals. No struggles. Just… this.”

I felt a cold dread settle in my chest. “But… I don’t understand. Isn’t this what everyone wants? To be free of pain? Free of stress?”

“For a while, maybe,” he said. “But forever? Without meaning? Without growth? That’s not peace. That’s stagnation. That’s… hell.”

I looked around, the golden light suddenly feeling oppressive, the smiles of the people hollow. “So… what now?”

He sighed again, his expression pained. “Now, you stay. And you learn. Or you don’t. Either way, this is your eternity.”

And with that, he walked away, leaving me standing in the perfect, unbearable stillness of my own making.

The locket pulsed faintly, and before I could think better of it, I pressed the small button on its side. The room was a void, a cavern of shadows so thick it felt like the darkness had weight, pressing against my skin. I woke abruptly, my heart thudding in my chest, though I couldn’t remember why. My arm dangled over the edge of the bed, fingertips brushing the cool wooden floor. And then it happened.

Something seized my hand.

It wasn’t human. I knew that immediately. The grip was too cold, too deliberate, the texture of its touch unfamiliar—smooth yet jagged, like polished stone with edges that bit into my palm. My breath hitched, but I didn’t pull away. Instinct, or perhaps some deep, primal understanding, told me that this was a moment of reckoning. First impressions mattered. And in the absence of sight, touch was everything.

I tightened my grip.

I could feel it now, not just in my hand but in the air around me, a presence that seemed to coil and uncoil like smoke. It was testing me. Waiting. I sat up slowly, my free hand fumbling for the lamp on my nightstand. The click of the switch was deafening in the silence, but the light didn’t come. The bulb remained dark, as though the shadows had swallowed it whole.

“Alright,” I whispered, my voice steadier than I expected. “Let’s do this.”

I swung my legs over the side of the bed, my feet meeting the floor with a soft thud. The thing still held my hand, its grip now less forceful, more curious. I stood, my knees trembling but my resolve firm. If this was a test, I wasn’t going to fail. I gave its hand—if it could be called that—a firm shake, the kind I’d practiced in front of a mirror before job interviews. Confident. Assured. Dominant.

The darkness shifted.

It wasn’t a movement I could see, but I felt it, a ripple in the air that made the hairs on my arms stand on end. The thing’s grip tightened again, but this time it wasn’t threatening. It was… reciprocating. A handshake. An agreement. The shadows around me seemed to pulse, and for a moment, I thought I heard something—a low, resonant hum, like the sound of distant thunder or the deep, mournful note of a cello.

And then it was gone.

The room was suddenly lighter, the oppressive darkness lifting like a curtain. My hand felt cold, but it was empty now, the strange presence vanished as quickly as it had appeared. I stood there for a long time, staring into the space where it had been, my mind racing. What had just happened? Had I imagined it? No. The ache in my palm was real, the memory of that grip etched into my skin.

I climbed back into bed, my heart still pounding but my thoughts strangely calm. Whatever that thing was, it had come for a reason. And I had met it—not with fear, but with strength. As I lay there, staring at the ceiling, I realized something: the darkness didn’t feel so heavy anymore. It felt… familiar. Almost comforting.

And when I closed my eyes, I dreamed of hands reaching out, not to seize, but to connect.

text:
The bookstore was quiet, the kind of quiet that feels like a held breath. The air smelled of paper and ink, and the faint hum of a coffee machine from the café in the corner buzzed in the background. I stood in front of the display, my fingers brushing against the glossy cover of *The Edge of Tomorrow* by Evelyn Carter. My Evelyn. My partner of ten years. The love of my life. The woman whose late-night typing had become the soundtrack to our shared existence.

I picked up the book, feeling the weight of it in my hands. It was strange, holding something so tangible that had once been nothing more than a series of late-night conversations and scattered pages on our kitchen table. Evelyn had handed me drafts over the years—fragments of chapters, character sketches, the occasional poetic line she was particularly proud of. I’d read them all, nodding, smiling, offering encouragement. But the truth was, I never really connected with her writing. It was dense, abstract, full of metaphors that felt like riddles. I loved her, so I lied. “It’s brilliant,” I’d say. And maybe it was. Just not to me.

But this book—this published, polished thing—was different. The cover was striking, a swirl of dark blues and golds, with a single, stark tree silhouetted against a stormy sky. The blurb on the back promised “a haunting exploration of love, loss, and the fragility of human connection.” I flipped it open, my eyes skimming the first page. And then the next. And the next.

By the time I reached the third chapter, I was sitting on the floor, my back against the shelf, completely unaware of the world around me. This wasn’t the Evelyn I knew. This wasn’t the abstract, meandering prose she’d shared with me. This was raw, visceral, alive. The characters were flawed and real, their pain so palpable it made my chest ache. The story was about a couple—two people who loved each other deeply but were slowly unraveling under the weight of unspoken truths. It was about the lies we tell to protect the ones we love, and the cost of those lies.

I read a passage where the protagonist, a man named Daniel, watches his partner, Claire, sleep. He thinks about all the things he’s never said to her, all the ways he’s failed her, all the love he still feels but can’t seem to express. My throat tightened. It was us. It was *us*. The late-night arguments we’d brushed under the rug, the quiet moments of doubt, the way we sometimes felt like strangers in the same bed. Evelyn had written *us* into this story, and she’d done it with a clarity that left me breathless.

I closed the book, my hands trembling. For the first time, I understood why she’d been so secretive about the final draft, why she’d stopped sharing pages with me. This wasn’t just a book. It was a confession. A mirror. A love letter and a goodbye, all at once.

That night, I sat across from her at the dinner table, the book between us. She looked at it, then at me, her eyes wide and uncertain. “You bought it,” she said softly.

“I did,” I replied. “And I read it.”

She swallowed, her fingers twisting in her lap. “And?”

I reached across the table, taking her hand in mine. “It’s the most beautiful thing you’ve ever written.”

Tears filled her eyes, and for a moment, neither of us spoke. The silence between us was heavy, but for the first time in a long time, it felt honest. And maybe, just maybe, that was enough.

text:
The photo trembled in my hands, its edges frayed and yellowed with age. It was a relic from a time before me, a snapshot of my wife, Clara, as a child. She stood between her parents, her smile wide and innocent, her eyes bright with the unburdened joy of youth. But it wasn’t Clara who made my blood run cold—it was the girl standing beside her, identical in every way, from the dimple in her left cheek to the way her hair curled at the ends. Twins. Clara had never mentioned a twin.

My mind raced, clawing through memories like a desperate animal. Clara’s sister, Evelyn, had been murdered shortly after we married—a cold case that had haunted her for years. Clara had always been vague about her, deflecting my questions with a shrug or a change of subject. “We weren’t close,” she’d say, her voice tight, her eyes distant. I’d assumed it was grief that made her withdraw, that her strange behavior—the sleepless nights, the sudden tears, the way she’d sometimes stare at me as if I were a stranger—was just the weight of loss. But now, staring at the photo, I wondered if I’d been wrong.

The house was too quiet, the air thick with the scent of rain. Clara was in the kitchen, humming softly to herself as she washed dishes. I could see her reflection in the window, her movements slow and deliberate. She had been like this for weeks, ever since the anniversary of Evelyn’s death. At first, I thought it was just the grief resurfacing, but now I wasn’t so sure. There was something else, something darker, lurking beneath the surface.

I stepped into the kitchen, the photo still clutched in my hand. Clara turned, her smile fading as she saw my face. “What’s wrong?” she asked, her voice steady but her eyes darting to the photo.

“Why didn’t you tell me you had a twin?” I asked, my voice sharper than I intended.

Clara froze, her hands still dripping with soapy water. For a moment, she said nothing, her face a mask of calm. Then, slowly, she dried her hands on a towel and walked toward me. “It’s complicated,” she said finally, her voice barely above a whisper.

“Complicated?” I echoed, my frustration bubbling over. “Clara, your sister was murdered. You’ve been acting strange for weeks. And now I find out you had a twin? How is any of this not important enough to tell me?”

She looked away, her shoulders tense. “Evelyn and I… we weren’t just sisters. We were the same person, in a way. When she died, a part of me died too. I couldn’t talk about her. I still can’t.”

Her words hung in the air, heavy and unspoken. I wanted to believe her, to wrap her in my arms and tell her it was okay. But something in her eyes stopped me—a flicker of something I couldn’t quite place. Fear? Guilt? Or something else entirely?

That night, I lay awake, the photo on the nightstand staring back at me. Clara slept soundly beside me, her breathing even and calm. But I couldn’t shake the feeling that I was missing something, that the truth was closer than I realized. And as the hours ticked by, I couldn’t help but wonder: if Clara and Evelyn were truly identical in every way, how could I be sure the woman lying next to me was really my wife?

The thought sent a chill down my spine, and for the first time in years, I felt like a stranger in my own home.
